args.text: [lane-lynx] Risks of caching DNS (Domain Name System) answers for too long: (1) Stale addresses: users are sent to servers that have moved or been retired, causing failures. (2) Slow recovery: during an outage or failover, traffic keeps going to the dead address until the cache expires. (3) Prolonged security exposure: a poisoned or hijacked answer stays in the cache and keeps misdirecting users long after the fault is fixed.

[lane-lynx] Idempotent retries matter because networks fail in ways that leave the sender unsure whether a request worked, so retrying is often the only safe choice. If the request is idempotent, meaning repeating it gives the same result as doing it once, a retry cannot cause harm such as a double payment or a duplicated order.

[lane-lynx] (1) Larger keys: a UUIDv7 (a time-ordered unique identifier) takes 16 bytes, against 4 or 8 for a typical integer key, so indexes and related tables grow bigger. (2) Leaked timing: the first part of the value holds the creation time, so anyone who sees an identifier can work out roughly when the row was made. Ordering is also only approximate between machines whose clocks differ.

[lane-lynx] A write-ahead log is a record where a database writes each planned change to durable storage before it alters the main data files. If the system crashes part-way through, it can read the log on restart to finish or undo those changes, so no committed work is lost and the data is not left half-written.

[lane-lynx] Two reasons to pin a client version in a benchmark: (1) Repeatability: a client update can change speed, retry behaviour or defaults, so results from different runs would not be comparable. (2) Fair attribution: with the client held fixed, any change in the results can be put down to the system under test, not to a hidden difference in the client.

[lane-lynx] Backpressure is a way for a queue's consumer to signal producers to slow down or pause when work arrives faster than it can be handled. This stops the queue growing without limit, which protects memory and keeps delays predictable, instead of letting the system fall over under overload.

[lane-lynx] A cron job can run twice in these ways: (1) two servers each hold the same schedule, so both fire at the same moment; (2) a slow run is still going when the next scheduled run starts, so the two overlap. One guard is a lock: the job takes a lock (for example a database row or a lock file) before starting and exits quietly if another run already holds it.

[lane-lynx] A tombstone is a small marker saved in place of a deleted item in a replicated store. Rather than erasing the data straight away, the store records that it was deleted, so every copy hears about the deletion and an out-of-date copy cannot bring the item back. Tombstones are removed later, once all copies have seen them.

[lane-lynx] Two signs that a test is flaky rather than failing: (1) it passes and fails on the same code with no change in between, so a plain re-run gives a different result; (2) the failures depend on things outside the code, such as timing, test order, shared data or the machine it runs on, and they vanish when the test is run alone.

[lane-lynx] A lease-based lock gives a holder the lock for a set time, after which it expires. Clock skew means machines disagree about the current time. If the holder's clock runs slow, it believes it still holds the lease after the lock service has expired it and given it to someone else, so two holders act at once. A fencing token, a number that rises with each grant, lets the shared resource reject the older holder.
